t: #3301 Maximize the Total Height of Unique Towers
o: Assign distinct positive heights with height[i] ≤ maximumHeight[i], maximizing the sum. Greedy insight: process towers from tallest cap to shortest; each tower should take the largest height still available, which is min(its cap, previous assigned height − 1). For [2,3,4,3] sorted descending [4,3,3,2] we assign 4,3,2,1 → 10. If any tower would be forced below 1, return −1, as in [2,2,1].
k: Sorting caps in descending order and assigning each tower the largest feasible remaining height is optimal by an exchange argument.
Feasibility fails exactly when some tower would need height < 1, i.e., there are more towers demanding high values than values available.

a.i: After sorting descending, the tallest-cap tower takes min(cap, ∞) and each subsequent tower takes min(cap, prev − 1). Any other assignment can only lower the sum: giving a taller-cap tower less while a shorter-cap one takes more is exchangeable without loss.
s: Maintain prev = assigned height of the previous tower (∞ initially).
Set h = min(cap, prev − 1); if h < 1 return −1; add h to the total and set prev = h.
a.t: O(n log n) — dominated by sorting; the assignment pass is linear.
a.sp: O(1) extra (in-place sort), or O(n) depending on the language's sort.

w: This single greedy is the standard solution; prove it briefly with an exchange argument if asked. Pitfalls: forgetting the −1 (distinctness), missing the h < 1 failure case, and 32-bit overflow of the sum (up to 10^5 × 10^9). Follow-up: return the actual assignment, or handle towers with equal caps explicitly.
